upper: Start at the top line, a little right of center. Curve up and to the left, then down and around counterclockwise to the bottom line and back up to the top to close a tall oval. Without lifting, pull a slanted line straight down the right side to the bottom line and finish with a short upward stroke that can lead into the next letter.
lower: Start just below the midline on the right. Curve up and around to the left, down to the bottom line and back up to close a small oval at the midline. Trace back down the right side to the bottom line and finish with a little upstroke toward the next letter.
mistakes: The most common slip is leaving the oval open at the top, which turns a into a cursive u. Make sure the pencil closes the circle before it goes down the right side. Some kids also add a loop on the down stroke, which makes it look like an e.
joins: Lowercase a begins with the same round stroke as c, d, g, o and q, so the connector from the letter before climbs up to the midline and curves back over the top. It ends on the bottom line, so almost any letter can follow it easily.
tip: Teach a, c, d, g, o and q together. They all start with the same round stroke, so once a feels natural the rest come faster.
metaDescription: Learn cursive A with a free worksheet. Step-by-step strokes for capital and lowercase cursive a, common mistakes, and a trace-then-write PDF.

upper: Start at the top line and pull a slanted line down to the bottom line. Go back up the same line, then curve out to the right and around to the midline for the first bump. Tuck in a tiny loop at the midline, then make a slightly larger bump that curves down to the bottom line and back in to meet the stem.
lower: Start on the bottom line and swing up to the top line, loop back to the left and slant straight down to the bottom line. Curve up to the midline on the right, then finish with a small checkstroke, a little sideways stroke that stays at the midline instead of dropping back down.
mistakes: Leaving off the little checkstroke at the end makes b look like an l followed by a u. Keep the top loop narrow too; a wide loop can make the stem lean and the letter look tipped over.
joins: Lowercase b ends at the midline, not the bottom line, so the next letter connects with a stroke straight across the top. Pairs like br, bo and be take extra practice because the next letter has to start up high.
tip: Say the motion out loud as your child writes: "up, loop, down, up and over, little hook." The hook at the end is the part that gets forgotten.
metaDescription: Free cursive B worksheet for capital and lowercase b. See how each stroke goes, why the little hook matters, and print a trace-then-write sheet.

upper: Start just below the top line with a small hook: curve up, over and back to the left. Then curve down and around counterclockwise in a big open curve to the bottom line, and finish with a short upward stroke to the right.
lower: Start on the bottom line and swing up to the midline. Make a small hook back over the top, then curve down and around to the left to the bottom line, leaving the right side open. Finish with an upstroke to the right.
mistakes: If the hook at the top turns into a closed loop, c starts to look like an e or an a. Keep the hook small and the right side open. Watch that the bottom of the curve actually touches the bottom line.
joins: Like a, d, g, o and q, lowercase c is a round letter, so the stroke coming into it rises to the midline and folds back over the top. It ends on the bottom line, which makes it easy to connect to whatever comes next.
tip: Practice a row of small c shapes with no pencil lifts between them. It is the base of six lowercase letters.
metaDescription: Free cursive C worksheet: how to write capital and lowercase cursive c, with the small top hook explained. Trace, then write. Printable PDF.

upper: Start at the top line and slant down to the bottom line. Make a small loop at the bottom, then curve out to the right and all the way up and around to the top line, coming back to the left to close the letter at the top. Finish with a small loop where the curve meets the stem.
lower: Start just below the midline and curve up, left and around counterclockwise to make a small oval, just like a. Then keep going straight up to the top line, trace back down the same line to the bottom line, and finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: Adding a loop on the tall stem turns d into a cursive c and l side by side. The stem should go up and come straight back down on itself. Also check that the oval is closed before the stem starts.
joins: Lowercase d connects easily on both sides: it starts with the round stroke of the a family and ends on the bottom line. In many traditional styles capital D does not join the letter after it, so leave a small space before the next letter.
tip: Think of lowercase d as an a with a tall stem. If your child can write a, they only need one more step.
metaDescription: Free cursive D worksheet with stroke-by-stroke help for capital and lowercase cursive d. Learn why the stem has no loop, then print a PDF.

upper: Start just below the top line. Curve up, around to the left and down to the midline to make the top curve. Tuck in a small loop at the midline, then make a larger curve down and around to the bottom line. Finish with a short stroke out to the right. It looks a bit like a backward 3.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to just below the midline. Loop back to the left, then curve down to the bottom line, crossing your first stroke. Finish with an upstroke to the right. The loop should be small and stay under the midline.
mistakes: A loop that goes all the way to the top line makes e look like an l. A loop that never opens up looks like an i. Keep the loop small and round, and stop it just under the dashed midline.
joins: Lowercase e is one of the easiest letters to join because it starts and ends on the bottom line. After b, o, v and w, though, the connector comes in at the midline, so the loop of the e gets very small. Practice oe, ve and we on purpose.
tip: Have your child write a row of eeeee without lifting. It builds the smooth up-and-loop rhythm that cursive depends on.
metaDescription: How to write cursive E, capital and lowercase, with simple stroke steps and the loop size that keeps e from looking like l. Free printable.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form. First make the cap: a wavy stroke across the top line, going left to right. Then start just below that cap, pull a slanted stroke down to the bottom line and curve it back to the left. Lift, and cross it near the midline with a short straight line.
lower: Start on the bottom line and swing up to the top line into a narrow loop. Slant straight down past the bottom line into the space below. Make a second loop that comes back up on the right side and closes at the bottom line, then finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: The lower loop sometimes ends up on the left side, which makes the f look backward. The tail should swing to the right and close where it meets the bottom line. Keep both loops thin so the letter stays tall and narrow.
joins: Lowercase f ends on the bottom line with an upstroke, so it joins easily to the next letter. Capital F usually stands alone in traditional cursive. Leave a small space before the next letter.
tip: Lowercase f is the only letter with a loop above the top half and a loop below the bottom line. Point that out, and it becomes easier to remember.
metaDescription: Free cursive F worksheet. Learn the traditional capital cursive F and the two-loop lowercase f, step by step, then print a trace-then-write PDF.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form. Start on the bottom line and swing up to the top line, loop over and come back down to the bottom line to make a tall loop. Near the midline, swing out to the right in a small backward curve, come back in to the stem, and finish with a short stroke out to the right.
lower: Start just below the midline and make the small oval of a. Without lifting, pull a straight line down past the bottom line into the space below. Loop back to the left and come up to cross at the bottom line, then finish with an upstroke to the right.
mistakes: Swinging the lower loop to the right instead of the left turns g into a q. The descender loop on g closes on the left side. Make sure the oval at the top is closed too.
joins: Lowercase g joins on both sides: the connector comes up to the midline and folds over the top of the oval, and the lower loop carries the pencil back up to the bottom line for the next letter.
tip: Write g and q next to each other a few times so your child can feel the difference: g loops back left, q swings forward to the right.
metaDescription: How to write cursive G, capital and lowercase. Stroke steps for the traditional capital G, the looped lowercase g, and how to tell g from q.

upper: Start just below the top line with a small hook, then pull a slanted line down to the bottom line for the left side. Lift. Start at the top line on the right and slant down to the bottom line. Go back up a little and make a small loop to the left at the midline that crosses the first stroke, then finish with a stroke out to the right.
lower: Start on the bottom line and swing up to the top line, loop back to the left and slant down to the bottom line. Retrace up a short way, make a hump over to the right like an n, come down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: A short top loop makes h look like an n, and a hump that closes into a loop makes it look like a k. Keep the first loop tall and the hump open at the bottom.
joins: Lowercase h starts with the same loop stroke as b, e, f, k and l, and it ends on the bottom line, so it connects smoothly. The pairs th, sh and ch come up a lot in reading, so they are worth extra rows of practice.
tip: Lowercase h, k and l begin exactly the same way. Practice them as a set so the tall loop becomes automatic.
metaDescription: Free cursive H worksheet with stroke help for capital and lowercase cursive h. Learn the tall loop and the hump, then print a practice PDF.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form. Start a little below the midline on the left and swing up and to the right to the top line. Pull a slanted line down to the bottom line, curve back to the left and swing up across the stem, finishing with a short stroke out to the right.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to the midline. Retrace straight back down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke to the right. Once the whole word is written, go back and add the dot above the letter.
mistakes: Putting a loop in the upstroke turns i into an e. The stroke goes up and comes straight back down on itself. Dotting the i before finishing the word breaks the flow, so save the dots for last.
joins: Lowercase i is the simplest joiner: it starts and ends on the bottom line. Kids often find it easiest to learn i, u, w and t first, since they all start with the same upstroke.
tip: Make a game of it: write a whole row of connected i shapes, then go back and dot them all at the end.
metaDescription: Free cursive I worksheet. Learn the traditional capital cursive I and the simple lowercase i, when to add the dot, and print a PDF to trace.

upper: Start a little below the midline and swing up to the top line, curving over into a small loop. Pull a slanted line down through the bottom line into the space below. Loop back to the left and come up to cross at the bottom line, then finish with a stroke out to the right.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to the midline. Pull a straight line down past the bottom line, loop back to the left, and come up to cross at the bottom line. Finish with an upstroke, and add the dot once the word is done.
mistakes: A lower loop that never closes makes j look like a hook instead of a letter. Bring the loop back up so it crosses the down stroke at the bottom line. Remember the dot, too.
joins: Lowercase j starts with the same upstroke as i, and its loop carries the pencil back to the bottom line, so it joins neatly into the next letter. It rarely appears in the middle of words, so most practice is at the start of a word.
tip: Lowercase j is an i that keeps going below the line. Teach it right after i so the connection is obvious.
metaDescription: How to write cursive J, capital and lowercase, with easy stroke steps and the loop below the line explained. Free printable cursive J worksheet.

upper: Start just below the top line with a small hook, then pull a slanted line down to the bottom line. Lift. Start at the top line on the right and curve down and in toward the stem, meeting it near the midline. Tuck in a small loop, then curve back out and down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke.
lower: Start on the bottom line and swing up to the top line, loop back and slant down to the bottom line. Go back up toward the midline and make a small loop or tuck on the right, then slant down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: Making the second part a full rounded hump turns k into an h. Look for the little tuck at the midline before the leg kicks out to the bottom line. Keep the top loop tall and narrow.
joins: Lowercase k ends on the bottom line, so it connects easily. The tuck in the middle slows kids down at first, which is fine. Words with ck, like back and duck, are good practice for the join from c into k.
tip: If k keeps turning into h, have your child say "loop, down, up, tuck, kick" while writing. The tuck is what makes it a k.
metaDescription: Free cursive K worksheet for capital and lowercase k. Step-by-step strokes, the small tuck that sets k apart from h, and a printable PDF.

upper: Start just below the top line and curve up into a small loop at the top. Slant down to the bottom line, make a small flat loop at the bottom that sits on the line, and finish with a stroke out to the right along the bottom line.
lower: Start on the bottom line and swing up to the top line, loop back to the left and slant straight down to the bottom line. Finish with an upstroke to the right. It is a taller, thinner version of the e motion.
mistakes: A short l looks just like an e. The loop has to reach all the way to the top line. Keep the down stroke straight and slanted the same way as the letters around it.
joins: Lowercase l connects smoothly on both sides because it starts and ends on the bottom line. Double l, as in ball and hill, is a good test of whether both loops come out the same height.
tip: Write e and l next to each other: same motion, different height. It helps kids see why the loop size matters.
metaDescription: Free cursive L worksheet. Learn capital cursive L with its top and bottom loops and the tall lowercase l, then trace and write on a free PDF.

upper: Start with a small hook, then make a hump up to the top line and pull a slanted line down to the bottom line. Go back up the line, make a second hump to the top line and come down. Make a third, smaller hump and finish with an upstroke at the bottom line.
lower: Start on the bottom line with a small hump up to the midline, then slant straight down to the bottom line. Go back up the line, make a second hump and come down, then a third hump, and finish with an upstroke. Lowercase m has three humps when you count the starting one.
mistakes: Kids often add an extra hump or leave one off. Count them out loud. Humps that come to a point instead of a round top can make m look like a row of i shapes.
joins: Lowercase m starts with an overcurve hump, the same way as n, v, x, y and z, and ends on the bottom line. After b, o, v or w the starting hump comes from the midline, so om and wm feel different from am.
tip: Practice n first. Once two humps feel smooth, m is the same letter with one more.
metaDescription: How to write cursive M, capital and lowercase, hump by hump. Free cursive M worksheet with common mistakes and a trace-then-write PDF.

upper: Start with a small hook, then make a hump up to the top line and pull a slanted line down to the bottom line. Go back up the line, make a second hump to the top line and come down to the bottom line. Finish with a short upstroke to the right.
lower: Start on the bottom line with a small hump up to the midline, then slant straight down to the bottom line. Go back up the line, make a second hump and come down to the bottom line, then finish with an upstroke to the right.
mistakes: Pointed tops make n look like a u turned upside down, or like a cursive v. Round the tops of the humps, and come straight back down each stroke instead of making loops.
joins: Lowercase n begins with an overcurve hump and ends on the bottom line, so it links neatly into most letters. It is one of the most common letters in English, which makes it a good one to get smooth early.
tip: Have your child trace a row of connected n shapes. The up-over-down rhythm carries straight over to m, v, x and y.
metaDescription: Free cursive N worksheet with simple steps for capital and lowercase cursive n. Round humps, common mistakes, and a printable practice sheet.

upper: Start at the top line, a little right of center. Curve up and to the left, then down and around counterclockwise to the bottom line and back up to close at the top. Finish with a small loop inside the top of the letter and a short stroke out to the right.
lower: Start just below the midline on the right and curve up, left and around counterclockwise to make a small oval that closes at the midline. Finish with a small checkstroke, a short sideways stroke at the midline that does not drop back down.
mistakes: Dropping the end of the o down to the bottom line makes it look like an a. The checkstroke stays up at the midline. Keep the oval closed at the top so it does not read as a u.
joins: Lowercase o ends at the midline, like b, v and w, so the next letter starts from up high. Pairs like or, os and oe are tricky because r, s and e change shape a little when they follow o. Capital O usually stands alone, with no join.
tip: Practice the two-letter pairs that trip kids up: on, or, os and oo. They show up in hundreds of common words.
metaDescription: How to write cursive O, capital and lowercase, and why lowercase o ends at the midline. Free cursive O worksheet to trace, then write.

upper: Start at the top line and pull a slanted line down to the bottom line. Go back up the same line to the top, then curve out to the right and around to the midline, coming back to close against the stem. Capital P usually does not join the next letter.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to the midline. Pull a straight line down past the bottom line into the space below, then retrace up to the midline. Make a forward hump that curves around to close at the bottom line, and finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: Leaving the bowl open at the bottom makes p hard to read. Bring the curve all the way back to the stem at the bottom line. Keep the stem straight; a loop in it makes p look like f.
joins: Lowercase p ends on the bottom line after closing its bowl, so it connects easily to the next letter. Capital P is usually written as a stand-alone letter, so leave a small space after it.
tip: Lowercase p retraces its own line, going down below the line and coming straight back up. Slow down on the retrace so the two strokes sit on top of each other.
metaDescription: Free cursive P worksheet for capital and lowercase p. Learn the retrace and the closed bowl step by step, then print a free practice PDF.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form, and it looks a lot like the number 2. Start with a hump up to the top line and pull a slanted line down to the bottom line. Make a small loop at the bottom, then finish with a stroke out to the right along the bottom line.
lower: Start just below the midline and make the small oval of a. Pull a straight line down past the bottom line, then swing the bottom of the stroke forward and up to the right so it closes at the bottom line, and finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: Looping back to the left turns q into a g. The tail of lowercase q swings forward, to the right. Capital Q is easy to mix up with a 2, so practice it inside words like Queen.
joins: Lowercase q is almost always followed by u, so practice qu as a pair. The forward swing at the bottom carries the pencil right into the upstroke of the u.
tip: If your child's school teaches a different capital Q, such as an O with a tail, follow the school. Both are correct; the traditional form is just the one most people learned.
metaDescription: How to write cursive Q, capital and lowercase. See the traditional capital Q that looks like a 2, the forward-swinging lowercase q, and print a PDF.

upper: Start at the top line and pull a slanted line down to the bottom line. Go back up the line, curve out to the right and around to the midline like a P, and tuck in a small loop at the stem. Then kick a slanted leg out to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to just above the midline. Make a tiny flat step to the right, called a shoulder, then slant straight down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: Skipping the shoulder makes r look like an i with no dot, or like a v. The little step at the top is what makes it an r. Keep it small so the letter does not get wide.
joins: Lowercase r ends on the bottom line and joins easily to the next letter. After b, o, v and w it starts from the midline, so the shoulder is less obvious; practice or and br by themselves.
tip: Lowercase r is one of the letters that looks least like its printed version. Show your child the cursive and print r side by side so they can read it, too.
metaDescription: Free cursive R worksheet with stroke steps for capital and lowercase cursive r, including the small shoulder that makes r readable. Print a PDF.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form. Start on the bottom line and swing up to the top line in a long upstroke. Loop back and curve down to the left and around to the bottom line, then curve back up and in to close against the upstroke, finishing with a small stroke to the left.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to just above the midline. Curve down and around to the right, then back to the left to close at the bottom line, a little like a small rounded point. Finish with an upstroke out to the right.
mistakes: A lowercase s that is too wide or too round can look like an o or an a. Keep the top pointed and the bottom closed. Many kids also forget to close the bottom before moving on.
joins: Lowercase s ends on the bottom line and joins easily. Like r, it changes shape a little after o, b, v and w, because the connector comes in at the midline. Practice os and ws on their own.
tip: Cursive s and printed s look very different, which is why kids sometimes struggle to read it. Point out s in a few cursive words so they learn to spot it.
metaDescription: How to write cursive S, capital and lowercase. Free worksheet with easy stroke steps, common mistakes, and trace-then-write practice rows.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form. First make the cap: a wavy stroke across the top line, going left to right. Then start just below that cap, pull a slanted stroke down to the bottom line and curve it back to the left. Capital T usually does not join the next letter.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up past the midline, about three quarters of the way to the top line. Retrace straight back down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke. After the word is done, cross the t with a short line just above the midline.
mistakes: Adding a loop on the upstroke turns t into an l. The stroke goes up and comes straight back down on itself, and it stops short of the top line. Crossing too low makes it look like a plus sign.
joins: Lowercase t starts with an upstroke and ends on the bottom line, so it connects easily. The cross is added at the end of the word, like the dot on an i, so the pencil keeps moving through the word first.
tip: The cap of capital T and capital F is the same stroke. Teach them together, then add the crossbar to make F.
metaDescription: Free cursive T worksheet for capital and lowercase t. Learn the traditional capital T, when to cross the t, and print a practice PDF.

upper: Start with a small hook, then make a hump up to the top line and pull a slanted line down, curving at the bottom line. Swing up to the top line again, then slant straight down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to the midline. Slant down to the bottom line, curve up to the midline again, slant down once more, and finish with an upstroke. It is two connected i strokes without the dots.
mistakes: Rounded humps on top turn u into an n. The tops of u are points that sit on the midline, and the bottoms are round. Keep the two downstrokes slanted the same way.
joins: Lowercase u starts with the same upstroke as i, t and w and ends on the bottom line, so it is one of the easiest letters to join. It follows q almost every time, so practice qu as a pair.
tip: Show your child that u is pointy on top and round on the bottom, while n is round on top and pointy on the bottom. Writing them back to back helps.
metaDescription: How to write cursive U, capital and lowercase, with simple stroke steps and the trick for telling u from n. Free printable cursive U sheet.

upper: Start with a small hook, then make a hump up to the top line and slant down to the bottom line. Slant back up to the top line on the right and finish with a small curl at the top. Capital V usually does not join the next letter.
lower: Start on the bottom line with a small hump up to the midline, then slant down to the bottom line. Curve back up to the midline and finish with a small checkstroke, a short sideways stroke that stays at the midline.
mistakes: Without the checkstroke, v looks like a u that is missing its last line. Make sure the end of the letter stays up at the midline instead of dropping back down.
joins: Lowercase v ends at the midline, like b, o and w, so the next letter connects with a stroke straight across the top. Words like have, give and very are good practice for the ve join.
tip: Practice b, o, v and w as their own group. They all end with the same little checkstroke at the midline.
metaDescription: Free cursive V worksheet with steps for capital and lowercase cursive v and the midline checkstroke that ends it. Trace, then write. PDF.

upper: Start with a small hook, then make a hump up to the top line and slant down to the bottom line. Slant up toward the top line, back down to the bottom line, and up to the top line again. Finish with a small curl. Capital W usually stands alone.
lower: Start on the bottom line and slant up to the midline. Slant down to the bottom line, curve up to the midline, down again, and back up to the midline. Finish with a small checkstroke that stays at the midline.
mistakes: Lowercase w often ends up with an extra point. Count the three upstrokes. Dropping the end to the bottom line makes it look like a u followed by an i.
joins: Lowercase w ends at the midline, so the next letter joins across the top. Pairs like we, wo and wr can feel awkward at first; practice them as two-letter chunks.
tip: Think of w as a u with one more upstroke and a little hook at the end.
metaDescription: How to write cursive W, capital and lowercase, step by step. Free cursive W worksheet with the tricky we and wo joins explained. Printable PDF.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form. Start with a small hook, make a hump up to the top line and curve down to the bottom line, finishing with a small stroke to the right. Lift. Then slant a straight line from the top line on the right down to the bottom line on the left so it crosses the first stroke.
lower: Start on the bottom line with a small hump up to the midline, then slant down to the bottom line and finish with an upstroke. When the word is done, go back and cross it with a slanted line from the midline on the right down to the bottom line on the left.
mistakes: Crossing the x before finishing the word breaks the flow, so save it for last, like dotting i. Make the cross slant the other way from the first stroke so the letter makes a clear X shape.
joins: Lowercase x starts with an overcurve hump like n and ends on the bottom line, so it joins easily. It shows up mostly at the end of words like box and fox, which makes it good practice for ox.
tip: Have your child write the word box in cursive. It covers the o checkstroke, the join into x, and the cross at the end.
metaDescription: Free cursive X worksheet. Learn to write capital and lowercase cursive x, when to add the crossing stroke, and print a practice PDF.

upper: Start with a small hook, then make a hump up to the top line and slant down, curving at the bottom line. Swing up to the top line again, then slant down past the bottom line. Loop back to the left and come up to cross at the bottom line, finishing with an upstroke.
lower: Start on the bottom line with a small hump up to the midline, then slant down to the bottom line. Curve back up to the midline, slant straight down below the bottom line, loop back to the left, and come up to cross at the bottom line. Finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: Stopping at the bottom line instead of going below it makes y look like a u. Let the second stroke drop all the way down, and close the loop so it crosses at the bottom line.
joins: Lowercase y joins on both sides: it starts with a hump like n and its lower loop carries the pencil back up to the bottom line. It often comes at the end of a word, as in happy and baby.
tip: Lowercase y is the first half of a u plus the lower loop of a j. Pointing that out helps kids put it together.
metaDescription: How to write cursive Y, capital and lowercase. Free cursive Y worksheet with the loop below the line explained, plus trace-then-write rows.

upper: Styles vary; this is the traditional form. Start with a small curve at the top line, then slant down to the bottom line. Make a small loop at the bottom line, then curve down below the line into a loop that comes back up to cross at the bottom line. Finish with an upstroke.
lower: Start on the bottom line with a small hump up to the midline, then slant down to the bottom line. Make a tiny loop on the bottom line, then curve down below the line into a loop that comes back up to cross at the bottom line. Finish with an upstroke.
mistakes: Kids often write cursive z like a printed z or the number 3. In traditional cursive, z dips below the bottom line with a loop. Some schools teach a z that stays on the line; follow your child's class if so.
joins: Lowercase z joins on both sides like y: it starts with a hump and its lower loop brings the pencil back to the bottom line. It is rare in English, so practice it in words like zoo, zebra and pizza.
tip: Lowercase z is one of the least familiar cursive letters, even for adults. A few rows of zoo and zebra are enough to make it stick.
metaDescription: Free cursive Z worksheet for capital and lowercase z. Learn the traditional looped cursive Z step by step, then print a trace-then-write PDF.
